title: Al-Falaq: the daybreak
hook: refuge with the Lord of the dawn from darkness, knots and envy (Surah 113)

segments.voice: Yesterday: An-Nas, the last surah, and the whisperer who draws back when Allah is remembered. Your line was the whisperer withdraws. Today, its twin. Day one hundred sixty.

Before dawn, for a long time, it's simply dark. Then a thin gray line opens along the horizon, like a seam splitting, and the night that felt endless turns out to have an edge. Yesterday's surah was about the danger inside, the whisper. Its twin, the surah just before it, is about dangers from outside: the dark, harm done in secret, other people's envy. And it names the One it turns to in a striking way. Not the Lord of the night. The Lord of the break.
screen: `A GRAY LINE ON THE HORIZON.` → `THE NIGHT HAS AN EDGE.` → `THE LORD OF THE BREAK.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred thirteen opens, in Pickthall's translation: Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the Daybreak. Falaq comes from a root meaning to split. The same root describes a seed splitting open to sprout, and the dawn splitting the dark. So the first thing the surah tells you about the One you run to is that He breaks the night open. Then it names four things to seek refuge from. First, the evil in what He created, a general line covering anything that can go wrong in a created world. Second, the darkness when it settles in, the night, and everything that feels bigger in it. Third, those who blow on knots. Commentators explain this as sorcery, the practice of tying knots and breathing spells on them. Classical scholars held that such harm is real and Allah's protection greater; some modern readers take the knots more figuratively. Fourth, the envier when he envies. Scholars define this envy as more than wanting what someone has: it's wanting them not to have it. The surah doesn't ask you to fight any of these yourself. It asks you to say: I seek refuge. An-Nas and Al-Falaq together are called al-mu'awwidhatan, the two refuge surahs. A hadith of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi says that reciting them with al-Ikhlas three times in the morning and three in the evening is enough protection for everything. Yesterday's surah went with him into sleep. This one's name makes it easy to pair with first light, though the hadith keeps both for morning and evening alike.
screen: `FALAQ — TO SPLIT, LIKE A SEED OR DAWN.` · `FOUR THINGS TO SEEK REFUGE FROM.` · `ENVY — WANTING THEM NOT TO HAVE IT.` · `THE TWO REFUGE SURAHS.` · then, large: `LORD OF THE DAYBREAK.`

segments.voice: Picture the first gray light of a dawn you've seen, and hold it. Then bring in one thing about the day ahead that feels like the dark, a meeting, a worry, a person who wishes you ill, and without solving it, set it in front of the light. If you pray, you can say the first line: qul a'udhu bi rabbil-falaq.
Al-Falaq. The daybreak, from a root meaning to split open, the name of Surah one hundred thirteen. Today's word.
Your line: lord of the daybreak. Even the longest night has an edge. One hundred sixty days now.

howItsDone: Muslims who keep the morning and evening remembrances recite al-Falaq with an-Nas and al-Ikhlas three times each morning and evening, and also after the prayers and before sleep, following the hadith.

Sorcery: the script says Muslims hold such harm is real and Allah's protection greater; some modern Muslims read 'blowers on knots' more figuratively (e.g. those who sow discord). Keeper may wish to add that.
Surah 113 is placed before 114 in the mushaf; the script calls it 'the surah just before it'.
